strengths: The paper addresses a timely and highly relevant NLP problem: unifying fragmented work on citation, attribution, and quotation in evidence-based LLM text generation.
It provides a broad empirical map of 134 papers, 300 evaluation metrics, 17 frameworks, 231 datasets, and 11 benchmarks, with an annotated dataset promised in a public repository.

The methodology is more explicit than many surveys: it defines research questions, databases, inclusion criteria, deduplication, independent screening, and an iteratively refined categorization scheme.
The taxonomy is useful and reasonably comprehensive, distinguishing parametric from non-parametric attribution, training from prompting, several citation characteristics, and downstream tasks.
The evaluation section effectively highlights the field's fragmentation, heterogeneous metrics, limited benchmark reuse, and lack of standardized evaluation protocols.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, and Figures 1, 4, and 7 help communicate the overall pipeline and conceptual structure.
weaknesses: Confidence in a main-conference recommendation is limited by the literature-search design. The query only combines LLM terms with citation, attribution, or quote and is matched only to titles and abstracts; it may miss work using terms such as RAG, grounding, provenance, evidence, source linking, fact verification, or attributed generation.

The claim of comprehensiveness is therefore somewhat stronger than the evidence supports. The paper should report broader search terms, snowballing, pilot recall tests, or a comparison against known seed papers.

Review rigor and reproducibility would be strengthened by a PRISMA-style flow diagram, exclusion-reason counts, database-specific query dates and logs, the annotation manual, and an inter-annotator agreement measure for screening and taxonomy labeling.

Table 1 requires clarification: the per-database counts sum exactly to 134 even though papers are often indexed in multiple sources, such as arXiv and ACL Anthology. The deduplication and source-assignment rule should be explained.
Several figures report counts that sum to more than 134 because of multi-label coding, but the denominators and overlap rules for percentages are not always clear.

Some taxonomy boundaries remain ambiguous, particularly post-retrieval versus in-context attribution and in-generation versus post-generation attribution; clearer definitions and decision rules would reduce annotation subjectivity.

The synthesis is mainly descriptive and frequency-based. It does not critically appraise study quality or compare which methods empirically improve citation correctness, attribution, or hallucination, and the proposed future directions remain relatively high-level.
Although a Git repository is promised, the manuscript should include a persistent URL or archived snapshot, specify the released fields, and ensure the resource is available without authentication.

strengths: The survey addresses a timely and important problem: the fragmented terminology and evaluation practices surrounding attribution, citation, quotation, grounding, and RAG-based text generation.

The review is comparatively systematic: it uses a PRISMA-style flow, explicit inclusion criteria, nine literature databases, a sensitivity analysis, inter-annotator agreement, and consensus resolution for uncertain cases.
The faceted taxonomy of attribution approach, citation characteristics, and task is clear, reusable, and appropriately allows multi-label annotations for systems that combine mechanisms.

The resource inventory is substantial, covering 134 papers, 300 extracted metrics, 19 frameworks, 11 benchmarks, and 231 datasets; the promised annotated dataset should materially support future research.
The paper is well organized and readable, with useful illustrative examples, trend summaries, and practical evaluation guidelines distinguishing core from contextual evaluation dimensions.
weaknesses: The conceptual contribution is primarily an integration and extension of prior categorizations by Huang and Chang, Li et al., and related RAG/grounding surveys. The novelty of the taxonomy and the narrow basis for the 'first survey' claim should be stated more explicitly.

The search strategy may omit relevant work. The main string relies on 'citation,' 'attribution,' or 'quote,' while related work may be described as RAG, grounding, provenance, verification, or evidence linking. English-language, publicly accessible, and full-text restrictions create further coverage bias.

Some counting and reporting details are under-specified. Percentages often exceed 100 because of multi-label assignment, but denominators and counting rules are not always clear; similarly, it is unclear whether the 300 'distinct metrics' include implementation variants or repeated metrics across tasks.

The analysis is mainly descriptive and does not appraise the quality of included studies or meta-evaluate whether the surveyed metrics actually measure the constructs they claim to measure. Sparse categories such as in-generation attribution, quotations, graphs, tables, and visuals limit the strength of several trend conclusions.

The screening workflow appears to split papers between annotators rather than independently screening all records, and the perfect inclusion agreement on a sample does not fully rule out screening errors. The provenance of the 134 papers across overlapping databases is also unclear because Table 2 sums exactly to 134.

For a 2026 venue, the February 2025 search should be updated to cover recent work on agentic, long-context, multimodal, and retrieval-integrated systems. In the provided manuscript, the repository link is only a generic https://github.com/ URL, so a working anonymized or final artifact link is needed for reproducibility.
